lede: The 10-year touched a 24-year high, then reversed; October hike odds fall to 30% ahead of payrolls.
geo_headlines: THE 10-YEAR HIT A 24-YEAR HIGH, THEN BUYERS SHOWED UP. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34% Thursday, its highest since 2002, then reversed (Reuters). Treasury's curve closed the 10-year at 5.24% (-5bp) and the 2-year at 4.78% (-10bp), with the 30-year at 5.61%. **Dovish comments from Fed officials drove the 2-year rally, per Reuters.** The 2s10s curve steepened to 46bp. The 10-year TIPS yield fell 5bp to 2.88%.

OCTOBER HIKE ODDS DOWN AGAIN, TO 30%. FedWatch puts an October 28 hike at 29.9%, from 35.4% a day earlier and about 70% a week ago; a December hike is 82.7% priced. Today's jobs report decides whether that keeps falling.

PAYROLLS AT 8:30 AM. Reuters' survey expects 90,000 September jobs (range 35,000-180,000) after 162,000 in August, unemployment steady at 4.1% and average hourly earnings up 3.2% from a year ago. Economists estimate 50,000-80,000 a month keeps pace with population growth.

STOCKS EDGED UP AS YIELDS EASED. The S&P 500 rose 0.19% to 7,666.45 Thursday and the Nasdaq 100 0.31%; the Dow was flat. The S&P is 1.70% below its August 13 record and the Nasdaq 100 0.75% below its September 22 record. VIX 16.39. Accenture jumped 15.8% after results; McCormick fell 4.9%.

NIKE MISSED ON SALES. Nike earned 48 cents a share against 44 cents expected, but revenue of $11.21 billion missed $11.35 billion and fell 5% currency-neutral; it guided to a high-single-digit revenue decline this fiscal year. Shares were down nearly 9% premarket (Investing.com).

INFLATION IS STILL RUNNING HOT ABROAD. Euro-zone September inflation rose to 3.8%, above the 3.6% forecast and the highest in three years (Bloomberg). Tokyo core CPI rose 2.7% against a 2.4% forecast. French yields hit 14-year highs (Reuters). ISM manufacturing Thursday was 54.5, with prices paid jumping to 77.9 from 71.1.

IRAN: MORE TROOPS, A THIRD CARRIER; OIL LOWER THIS MORNING. The US is deploying thousands more troops and a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East (AP); Trump said "we blow them up or make a deal" (Politico). Brent December is $99.89 (-2.4%) after Thursday's 4.4% jump; WTI $89.28 (-3.9%). Asia was mixed: Hong Kong -2.7%, Nikkei -0.9%. Futures: Nasdaq +0.72%, S&P +0.48%.
client_frame_short: The bond market finally caught a break: the 10-year Treasury yield touched its highest level since 2002 on Thursday, then fell as buyers stepped in, and short-term yields dropped sharply on softer talk from Fed officials. **Markets now see under a one-in-three chance of an October rate hike.** Stocks edged higher Thursday and futures are up this morning, helped by oil slipping back below $100. Today's jobs report at 8:30 is the real test; a middling number keeps this calm intact, and nothing here calls for portfolio changes.
client_frame:
If a client calls before the jobs report, the story is a bond market that blinked, in a good way.

What happened: on Thursday morning the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34%, the highest since 2002. Then buyers stepped in, and it closed at 5.24%. Shorter-term yields fell more, after Fed officials said they wanted more data before raising rates again. Markets now put the chance of an October hike near 30%, down from about 70% a week ago. Stocks edged higher, and futures are up this morning.

Why it matters: high yields are attracting buyers. That is how bond markets are supposed to work, and it is a useful reminder for clients that 5% yields are an opportunity, not only a threat. A client holding cash or short-term Treasuries can now lock in yields near 5% for a decade, levels most investors have not seen in their careers.

What has not changed: inflation is still too high around the world. Europe's inflation rate jumped to 3.8%, Tokyo's beat forecasts, and American factories say their input prices rose sharply in September. Oil is still near $100 with the US sending another carrier to the Gulf. So this is a pause in the bond sell-off, not an all-clear. Nike also warned that its sales will shrink this year, citing weak demand in China and tougher competition, a reminder that not every consumer brand is thriving.

Today's test: economists expect about 90,000 jobs and 4.1% unemployment. A number near that keeps the calm. A strong number would likely push yields and hike odds back up; a weak one would pull them down further, with growth worries attached.

For clients, the message holds: lock in quality income at these yields, keep equity plans in place, and do not trade the jobs report. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40%, a 30-year above 5.75%, or payrolls strong enough to lift October hike odds back above 50%.
